### Question 1

Think about a cold going around your class versus a broken arm. A broken arm cannot jump to your friend; a cold can. 'Communicable' shares a root with 'communicate' - the germ gets passed along like a message. So the test is not how bad the illness is, how many people have it, or who is vulnerable to it. The only question is whether the agent can travel from its reservoir - a person, an animal, or a place like water or soil - into a new host.

### Question 2

Picture two different waiting rooms. Isolation is for people who definitely carry the agent, so we keep them apart to stop the handoff. Quarantine is for people who may have been infected during a known exposure and do not yet know - like benching a player who took a hit to the head until the trainer clears them. Quarantine means 'maybe, and we are watching'; isolation means 'yes, and we are containing.' Notice that neither word tells you anything about how the germ travels.

### Question 3

Every agent has a home address where it lives and makes copies of itself - that is the reservoir. It might be a person, a bat, a cow, or a pond. To interrupt an agent you ask three questions in order: where does it live (reservoir), how does it travel (mode of transmission), and how does it get in (portal of entry). The reservoir is the house, the mode of transmission is the trip, and the portal of entry is the front door of the next house.

### Question 4

Picture measles as a fire and immune people as soaked logs. When 95 of 100 logs are wet, a spark lands, sputters, and dies out. Drop to 80 wet logs and enough dry ones are now touching each other for the fire to hop across the pile and keep going. Nothing about the spark changed - only the fuel around it. The driest logs are babies too young for the shot and children on cancer treatment, who were safe only because the logs around them were soaked.

### Question 5

Incubation is the quiet stretch: the agent has moved in and is multiplying, but you feel nothing yet, like dough rising before it looks like bread. Communicability is whenever the agent is actually being shed into the world. Those are two separate stopwatches, and nothing forces them to start or stop together. When they overlap, someone can say 'I feel completely fine' and be telling the truth while still handing the agent to the next person.

### Question 6

A vector is a living delivery service. The mosquito is neither the germ nor a sick person - it picks the virus up from one body and injects it into another. Contaminated water also makes a delivery, but water is not alive, so that route is called a vehicle instead. The distinction is practical, not fussy: if the courier is alive you attack the courier with screens, repellent, and draining standing water, and quarantining people accomplishes nothing.

### Question 7

A diagnosed case is the last domino you can actually see fall. Contact tracing reaches the dominoes standing next to it and taps them: you were near someone infectious, here is a test, a preventive medication, or a plan for the next several days. The timing is the whole point - reach people during the quiet stretch, before they can pass anything on. And the index patient's name is never disclosed, because tracing only works if people are willing to name their contacts.

### Question 8

TB treatment runs for months, and it is the kind of treatment where stopping halfway is worse than never starting: the hardiest bacteria survive the partial course and their descendants shrug the drugs off. DOT is a coach watching each set get finished - someone confirms every dose actually goes down. It is not about distrust. Taking multiple pills daily for months is genuinely hard for anyone, and the cost of missed doses is not just a relapse, it is a strain that barely responds to treatment.

### Question 9

There is no single national rulebook. Each state writes its own list of conditions that clinicians and laboratories must report, and that piece is enforceable law. States then pass what they learn up to CDC by agreement, so CDC can assemble a national picture and compare jurisdictions using shared case definitions. Think of each town keeping a required weather log and then choosing to send it to the national forecast office - the logging is mandatory, the sharing upward is cooperative.

### Question 10

Some agents ride in heavy droplets that arc and fall within a few feet, like seeds someone spits - keep your distance, wear a mask, and you are largely covered. Measles rides on particles small enough to float, behaving more like smoke that still hangs in the room two hours after the person walked out. You cannot outrun smoke by standing farther away. You need a respirator that seals to your face and room air that is actively pulled out and filtered. Floating means airborne.

### Question 11

Elimination is getting every ant out of your kitchen. It is a real achievement, but ants still exist outside, so you keep the traps set and the crumbs swept or they walk right back in. Eradication is ants no longer existing anywhere on Earth - you throw the traps away and never think about it again. Smallpox is the only human disease we have ever done that to. Measles shows the difference painfully: the Americas held elimination for years and then lost it once coverage slipped and transmission restarted.

### Question 12

Vaccines teach the immune system to build its own antibodies, which takes time and requires an immune system mature enough to learn - so MMR is not used below 6 months. Immune globulin is different: it is ready-made antibody, borrowed protection handed over directly, which is why it still helps days after the exposure rather than only within 72 hours. That also explains why you do not give both at once: the borrowed antibody would neutralize the vaccine virus before the infant's own immune system ever saw it, wasting the dose.
